paragraphs.title: Opening of the Psalm and Praise of the King

easy.explanation: The psalm begins, “My heart is inditing a good matter.”
easy.q: What is the poet's heart inditing?

answers: The pen of a ready writer
easy.explanation: He says, “my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.”
easy.q: What does the poet compare his tongue to?

answers: He is fairer than the children of men
He is hidden from the people
He is dressed as a common soldier
easy.explanation: The king is described as “fairer than the children of men.”
easy.q: What is said about the king's appearance?

answers: He is composing a worthy song
He is recording a military defeat
medium.explanation: The phrase shows that the poet is moved to compose a good and honorable song.
medium.q: What does the phrase “inditing a good matter” show about the poet?

medium.explanation: A ready writer writes quickly and skillfully, emphasizing the fluency of the poet's words.
medium.q: What does the image of a “ready writer” emphasize?

answers: Because grace is poured into his lips
Because he has conquered every nation
medium.explanation: The verse connects God's blessing with the grace poured into the king's lips.
medium.q: Why has God blessed the king forever?

answers: The poem moves from the poet's composition to praise of the king
The poem moves from a wedding to a battle
The poem moves from judgment to lamentation
challenge.explanation: The poet first describes his song and then turns to praise the king.
challenge.q: What movement occurs in these verses?

challenge.explanation: The king is praised for his beauty, the grace of his lips, and God's blessing.
challenge.q: What combination best describes the king in this opening section?

answers: His words flow readily and purposefully
He cannot find words to speak
He is writing a legal accusation
challenge.explanation: The comparison suggests fluent speech directed toward a meaningful subject.
challenge.q: What does the poet's comparison of his tongue to a writer's pen suggest?

paragraphs.title: The King as a Warrior Who Rules Justly

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Gird thy sword upon thy thigh.”
easy.q: What is the king told to gird upon his thigh?

easy.explanation: The king rides because of truth, meekness, and righteousness.
easy.q: For what does the king ride prosperously?

easy.explanation: The verse says that the people fall under him because of his sharp arrows.
easy.q: What happens to the king's enemies because of his sharp arrows?

medium.explanation: The sceptre is called right, showing that the king's rule is upright and just.
The verse declares, “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.”
medium.q: How long is the king's throne said to endure?

answers: He loves righteousness and hates wickedness
He has many horses and arrows
medium.explanation: The anointing follows the statement that the king loves righteousness and hates wickedness.
medium.q: Why has God anointed the king with the oil of gladness?

answers: He is powerful in battle and committed to justice
He is wealthy but unwilling to lead
He is peaceful because he lacks authority
challenge.explanation: The passage presents the king as a mighty warrior whose rule is also founded on moral righteousness.
challenge.q: Which description best combines the king's military and moral qualities?

answers: The king makes a clear moral distinction
The king refuses to judge right and wrong
The king values appearance above character
challenge.explanation: These statements show that the king's character and rule are morally discerning.
challenge.q: What contrast is established by loving righteousness and hating wickedness?

answers: The arrows show his victory, while the sceptre shows his just rule
Both symbols show that he is a priest
The arrows show weakness, while the sceptre shows fear
challenge.explanation: The arrows represent power over enemies, while the right sceptre represents upright government.
challenge.q: How do the arrows and the sceptre contribute to the portrait of the king?

paragraphs.title: The King as Bridegroom and the Queen at His Right Hand

easy.explanation: The verse names myrrh, aloes, and cassia as the scents of his garments.
easy.q: What are the king's garments said to smell of?

easy.explanation: The queen stands “upon thy right hand.”
The verse specifically says that she stands in “gold of Ophir.”
easy.q: What kind of gold does the queen wear?

medium.explanation: The ivory palaces reinforce the luxurious and royal setting.
medium.q: What do the ivory palaces contribute to the description?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “Kings' daughters were among thy honourable women.”
medium.q: Who are among the king's honourable women?

answers: He is shown as a bridegroom in a royal celebration
He is shown as a prisoner
He is shown as a servant leaving the palace
medium.explanation: The perfumed garments, palace, and queen create the setting of a royal wedding.
medium.q: What change in the king's portrayal occurs here?

challenge.explanation: These details combine to create a richly ceremonial picture of royal splendor.
challenge.q: What do the perfumes, ivory palaces, and gold together communicate?

answers: She holds a place of honor and distinction
She is separated from the royal court
She is preparing to lead the army
challenge.explanation: Standing at the right hand signifies an honored and prominent position.
challenge.q: What does the queen's position at the king's right hand imply?

answers: It shifts from his warrior qualities to his royal and marital glory
It denies that he is a king
It changes the subject to the enemies' families
challenge.explanation: After describing his sword, arrows, and sceptre, the psalm presents his splendor as bridegroom and king.
challenge.q: How does this section relate to the earlier description of the king?

paragraphs.title: The Poet's Address to the Bride and the Wedding Procession

answers: Hearken, consider, and incline her ear
easy.explanation: She is told, “Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear.”
easy.q: What is the daughter told to do?

answers: Her own people and her father's house
easy.explanation: The verse says, “forget also thine own people, and thy father's house.”
easy.q: What is she told to forget?

easy.explanation: The daughter of Tyre comes with a gift.

medium.explanation: The verse says, “So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty.”
medium.q: What does the king greatly desire?

answers: As her Lord, whom she should worship
As her servant, whom she should command
As her enemy, whom she should avoid
medium.explanation: The verse calls him her Lord and tells her to worship him.
medium.q: How is the king described in relation to the bride?

answers: Wrought gold and raiment of needlework
medium.explanation: Her clothing is described as wrought gold and needlework.
medium.q: What kind of clothing does the king's daughter wear?

answers: She is entering a new household and royal identity
Her father's house has been destroyed
She is being sent away without honor
challenge.explanation: The command marks her transition from her former family and identity into her new life with the king.
challenge.q: What does the command to forget her father's house indicate?

answers: A joyful and honorable royal wedding
challenge.explanation: The gifts, garments, and attendants create a public and celebratory wedding atmosphere.
challenge.q: What atmosphere is created by the gifts, fine clothing, and procession?

answers: They show that her entrance is part of a formal procession
They show that the bride is being rejected
They indicate that the king has left the palace
challenge.explanation: The companions following her emphasize the ceremonial nature of her entrance.
challenge.q: What is significant about the virgins following the bride?

paragraphs.title: The Blessing of Continuity and Praise Through the Generations

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children.”
easy.q: Who will take the place of the king's fathers?

easy.explanation: He may make them “princes in all the earth.”
easy.q: What may the king make his children?

easy.explanation: The poet says, “I will make thy name to be remembered in all generations.”
easy.q: What will the poet make to be remembered in all generations?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to continuing remembrance through successive generations.

answers: They are appointed as princes throughout the earth
They leave the kingdom without authority
medium.explanation: Their appointment as princes extends the king's rule and influence.
medium.q: How do the children continue the king's influence?

answers: They will praise the king for ever and ever
They will forget the royal family
They will oppose the king's children
medium.explanation: The verse concludes, “therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever.”
medium.q: What will the people do because the name is remembered?

answers: Both express continuity beyond the present generation
Both focus on the defeat of enemies
challenge.explanation: The children preserve the royal line, while remembrance preserves the king's name through time.
challenge.q: What idea connects the king's children with remembrance through generations?

answers: From succession in the royal family to enduring praise
From a wedding procession to military preparations
From praise to the bride's return home
challenge.explanation: The verses move from the king's children and princes to remembrance and praise forever.
challenge.q: What is the main movement in the closing verses?

answers: The uncertainty of the royal succession
challenge.explanation: The language of forever stresses permanence and continuing honor.
challenge.q: What does the repeated idea of “for ever” emphasize?
